\chapter{Why, and Because}
\label{ch:ml-kaaranam}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask why something is so, and give a reason in speech or in writing.}

From cold: the question word and the two ways to answer it, which of them belongs in speech, and the word from chapter two that the question is built on.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[entukoṇṭŭ]{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്} (entukoṇṭŭ) — \textquotedblleft{}by what\textquotedblright{}, which is how Malayalam asks why}

\label{lesson:ML-C73-enthukondu}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for \emph{what}. You have had it since the second chapter, inside the question you ask for somebody's name.

Today it grows an ending, and becomes a different question.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} — \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} — \textbf{why}
\end{quote}

Look at the front of it. \textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}} is sitting there, the word you already have. What follows is \textbf{\ml{കൊണ്ട്}} (\emph{koṇṭŭ}), an ending that means \emph{by means of} — so the whole question asks, quite literally, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}by what?\textquotedblright{}}

That is worth noticing rather than memorising. \textbf{Malayalam did not invent a new word for \emph{why}; it took the word for \emph{what} and asked what caused the thing.}

Your question words now cover four of the five things a person asks about:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}} \emph{entŭ} & what \\
\textbf{\ml{ആര്}} \emph{ārŭ} & who \\
\textbf{\ml{എവിടെ}} \emph{eviṭe} & where \\
\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} & why \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{എന്തു}} is \emph{entŭ} with its final mark opened out, which is what this script does when something follows. \textbf{\ml{കൊണ്ട്}} is the piece carrying the meaning of \emph{with} or \emph{by}.

\textbf{Three of the four question words in that table open on \ml{എ}} — \emph{entŭ}, \emph{eviṭe} and now \emph{entukoṇṭŭ}. That is the letter the pointing chapter named as the one that asks: change a word's front from \ml{ഇ} to \ml{അ} to \ml{എ} and it walks from \emph{near} to \emph{far} to \emph{a question}. Today's word keeps the \ml{എ} because it is built on a word that had it already.

\textbf{\ml{ആര്}} is the odd one out and starts on \ml{ആ}. Question words are a family, not a rule — most of them carry the asking letter, and \emph{who} does not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entŭ} … \emph{entukoṇṭŭ}
  \item the four question words in the table
  \item which part of today's word you already had, and which part is new
  \item what the new part means on its own
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{why}? (\emph{\textbf{Entukoṇṭŭ}}.) Which word is hiding at the front of it? (\textbf{\ml{എന്ത്}} — \emph{what}.) And what does the ending add? (\textbf{By means of} — so the question is \textquotedblleft{}by what?\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāraṇaṁ]{\ml{കാരണം} (kāraṇaṁ) — a reason, and the answer to the question}

\label{lesson:ML-C73-kaaranam}



\begin{quote}
Ask \emph{why} in Malayalam. Say which word is hiding inside it.

Now you need something to answer with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{കാരണം}} — \emph{kāraṇaṁ} — \textbf{a reason; and so, \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}}
\end{quote}

It is a \textbf{noun} first. \emph{Kāraṇaṁ} is a reason, a cause, the thing behind something — and Malayalam then uses that same noun to join two statements, the way English uses \emph{the reason is} before sliding into \emph{because}.

The word is Sanskrit, \textbf{\dv{कारण}} (\emph{kāraṇa}), taken whole. That puts it in the same company as \textbf{\ml{ചിന്ത}}, the thought-noun that \emph{cintikkuka} stands on, and \textbf{\ml{സുപ്രഭാതം}}, the good-morning this book teaches — Malayalam borrows a Sanskrit noun and puts it to work without reshaping it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it sits between the two halves}]
Say the thing, then the word, then the reason:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
what happened & \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{ഇഷ്ടം}} \\
the joiner & \textbf{\ml{കാരണം}} \\
why & (your reason) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{This is the everyday one}, the word a person reaches for in speech. It asks nothing of the sentences on either side of it — neither half is rebuilt, the same way the quotative left a quoted sentence alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kāraṇaṁ}
  \item the question and the joiner one after the other — \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} … \emph{kāraṇaṁ}
  \item what the word means before it means \textquotedblleft{}because\textquotedblright{}
  \item two other Sanskrit nouns this book took whole
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{kāraṇaṁ} as a noun? (\textbf{A reason, a cause}.) What job does it do between two statements? (\textbf{Because}.) And what is the question it answers? (\emph{\textbf{Entukoṇṭŭ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[entukoṇṭennāl]{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ} (entukoṇṭennāl) — the long one, on the page}

\label{lesson:ML-C73-enthukondennaal}



\begin{quote}
Say the everyday word for \emph{because}.

Today's is the one you will read rather than say, and it is long enough to be worth taking slowly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}} — \emph{entukoṇṭennāl} — \textbf{because} (written, explaining)
\end{quote}

Put it beside the question from two pages ago and the first half is the same letters:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} & why \\
\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}} & because \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{The answer carries the question inside it.} That is the thing to see on the page — a long unfamiliar word with a word you know at the front of it stops being unfamiliar, and this one is signposted more clearly than most.

This book does not take the tail apart for you. The pieces after \textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} are read different ways by different grammars, and guessing between them would teach you something that might be wrong.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which one to use}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
speaking, everyday & \textbf{\ml{കാരണം}} \\
writing, explaining & \textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both join a statement to its reason and neither rebuilds either half. \textbf{Reach for \ml{കാരണം} when you talk.} Meeting the long one on a notice or in a written explanation is what this lesson is for, and a reader who can see the question word inside it has already got most of the way.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the long word and find the question word at its front
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} … \emph{entukoṇṭennāl}
  \item which of the two because-words you would use out loud
  \item why this book stops short of taking the ending apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}} mean? (\textbf{Because}.) Which word can you see at the front of it? (\textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} — \emph{why}.) And which because-word would you say rather than write? (\emph{\textbf{Kāraṇaṁ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kāraṇaṁ ōrmma]{(asking and answering why) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R73-cause-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Ask \emph{why}, and say which word you already had is sitting at the front of it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a question and two answers}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
to ask & \textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ട്}} \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} \\
to answer, speaking & \textbf{\ml{കാരണം}} \emph{kāraṇaṁ} \\
to answer, writing & \textbf{\ml{എന്തുകൊണ്ടെന്നാൽ}} \emph{entukoṇṭennāl} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Until this chapter, cause could not be handled in either direction.} There was no way to ask what was behind something and no way to give it. Three words close both halves at once, and two of the three are built on material you had: \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} on the word for \emph{what}, and the written one on \emph{entukoṇṭŭ} itself.

\textbf{\ml{കാരണം} is the one to have in your mouth.} The long one is for reading.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three words in the table
  \item which two of them share their opening letters, and why
  \item which one you would use out loud, and which on a notice
  \item the question word this chapter is built on, from chapter two
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask \emph{why}? (\emph{\textbf{Entukoṇṭŭ}}.) What does \emph{kāraṇaṁ} mean on its own, before it means \emph{because}? (\textbf{A reason}.) And which of the two because-words carries the question inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Entukoṇṭennāl}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
